cues.text: Welcome to MIT 8113, Digital Transformation and Innovation.
This is Study Session 5, Organisational Culture and KPIs for Transformation.
We begin with the first topic, organisational culture, and work through its models in order.
Organisational culture is the shared values, assumptions, norms and behaviours that guide how people work and make decisions.
Take each part in turn.
Values are what a group believes matters.
Assumptions are what people take for granted without discussing it.
Norms are the unwritten rules about what is acceptable.
Behaviours are what people actually do.
Together these guide how people work and decide.
Culture shows up in four places: what leaders reward, how information flows, how mistakes are treated, and how teams collaborate.
If leaders reward only speed, people learn that speed matters.
If information stays at the top, people learn to wait.
If mistakes are punished, people learn to hide them.
This leads to a key distinction.
Formal strategy says what an organisation intends.
Culture shapes what people actually do.
Culture can work for transformation or against it.
It can accelerate transformation through learning, trust, openness and shared purpose.
It can obstruct transformation through fear, silos, excessive hierarchy and resistance.
A silo is a part of the organisation that works in isolation and does not share information or goals with others.
The source also describes the digital-first organisation.
It does not simply use digital tools.
It uses digital capabilities as a default where appropriate, and it continuously improves how value is delivered.
Notice the qualification: physical and human channels may still be important.
Being digital-first does not mean abandoning branches, face-to-face service or personal contact where they serve the customer.
Now we turn to the Competing Values Framework, or CVF.
It rests on two questions.
The first is whether the organisation's focus is internal or external.
The second is whether it values flexibility or stability and control.
Combining the two gives four cultures.
The source presents them in a table with four columns: Culture, Focus, Strength and Risk.
We will go through the rows in order.
The first row is Clan culture.
Its focus is internal and flexible.
Its strength is teamwork, belonging and development.
Its risk is avoiding difficult decisions.
A group that cares so much about harmony may put off the hard choices.
The second row is Adhocracy.
Its focus is external and flexible.
Its strength is experimentation, entrepreneurship and innovation.
Its risk is weak controls if unmanaged.
The third row is Market culture.
Its focus is external and stable or control-oriented.
Its strength is results, competition and customer outcomes.
Its risk is pressure and short-termism, meaning too much attention on near-term results at the expense of longer-term health.
The fourth row is Hierarchy.
Its focus is internal and stable or control-oriented.
Its strength is procedures, consistency and accountability.
Its risk is bureaucracy and slow response.
Organisations combine these characteristics.
The source gives an example.
A regulated bank may need hierarchical controls for ledger integrity, because the accuracy of its accounting records cannot be left to chance.
The same bank may use adhocracy for low-risk product experiments, trying new ideas where a failure will not damage the core.
The lesson is that transformation does not require eliminating every formal control.
Next is Schein's three levels of culture.
Think of culture as having a visible surface and a hidden depth.
The first level is artefacts.
These are visible elements such as dashboards, dress, office layout and rituals.
You can see them as soon as you walk in.
The second level is espoused values.
These are stated beliefs and strategies, for example the phrase "customer first".
They are what the organisation says it believes.
The third level is basic underlying assumptions.
These are deeply held, often unconscious expectations.
One example is the assumption that mistakes are punished.
Nobody says it aloud, yet everyone behaves as if it were true.
This has a practical consequence.
Changing a collaboration tool changes artefacts.
Changing incentives, leadership behaviour and trust can shift deeper culture.
The source adds an illustration.
A team with an "innovation" poster may still hide problems if mistakes are punished.
The poster is an artefact and the assumption underneath is what drives behaviour.
Now Hofstede's cultural dimensions.
The source lists six.
First, power distance, which is the acceptance of unequal authority.
Second, individualism versus collectivism.
Third, masculinity versus femininity.
In the model's own terminology, this contrasts competition and achievement with cooperation and care.
Fourth, uncertainty avoidance.
Fifth, long-term versus short-term orientation.
Sixth, indulgence versus restraint.
These come with an important caution.
They describe broad cultural patterns, not deterministic individual traits.
They do not tell you how any one person will behave.
The source says to use them cautiously to support communication, inclusive teamwork and change management across contexts.
Finally, the source introduces Deal and Kennedy's model.
It examines two factors: risk level and speed of feedback.
Combining them gives four cultures.
Tough-guy or macho culture has high risk and rapid feedback.
Work-hard, play-hard culture has low risk and rapid feedback.
Bet-your-company culture has high risk and slow feedback.
Process culture has low risk and slow feedback.
The source gives a contrast to make this concrete.
A startup experiment may offer quick feedback, whereas a major infrastructure investment takes longer to evaluate.
The practical guidance is to match learning mechanisms to risk and feedback speed.
A fast experiment can be reviewed quickly and often.
A slow, high-stakes investment needs learning mechanisms suited to a longer wait for results.
